result: {"decisions":[{"point":"D1","problem":"How should interpretability researchers validate that their mechanistic insights are real and important rather than illusory or insubstantial?","did":"Advocated demonstrating downstream applications where interpretability methods beat non-interp baselines, as validation of insights.","alternatives_named":["Demo applications because we terminally care about them","Back-chain from desired end-states like solving alignment","Look for problems in the wild to apply methods to"],"stated_reason":"Solving a problem no one else can solve provides evidence that the insights are real and significant, and side-steps the lag between new claims and suitable validation paradigms.","quote":"Rather my claim is: Demonstrating your insights can be leveraged to solve a problem—even a toy problem—that no one else can solve provides *validation* of those insights."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to evaluate whether an interpretability technique gives a genuine advantage on a downstream task.","did":"Required a fair fight: specify the allowed affordances and compare against the best non-interp techniques using the same affordances.","alternatives_named":["Instructing the model to be more honest","Few-shot prompting with the honesty data","Finetuning the model on the honesty data"],"stated_reason":"Outperforming baselines under the same rules shows the insight does something practical rather than being illusory or narrow.","quote":"Clearly specify which affordances are allowed (e.g. in which ways are you allowed to interact with the model? what data are you allowed to use?)"},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether to accept saliency map results that look compelling as evidence of genuine mechanistic insight.","did":"Treated the compelling-looking results as illusory because a random-network ablation gave equally compelling results.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Results on an untrained random network were just as compelling, suggesting saliency maps act like simple edge detectors needing no mechanistic understanding.","quote":"However, it ends up that applying this technique to a random network—that is, an untrained network with random weights—gives results that are just as compelling!"},{"point":"D5","problem":"How to interpret the finding that a simple gendered-token-deletion baseline is competitive with SHIFT.","did":"Declined to dismiss the baseline and instead remained suspicious that SHIFT is just fancy token deletion until a task separates them.","alternatives_named":["Dismiss the baseline because it obviously wouldn't work on other similar tasks"],"stated_reason":"SHIFT might also fail on other tasks, so the baseline's likely lack of generality does not distinguish the two.","quote":"It's tempting to dismiss results like this, since obviously this \"gendered token deletion\" baseline wouldn't work on other similar tasks. But SHIFT might not either!"},{"point":"D2","problem":"Which baselines to compare SHIFT against on the spurious-cue removal task.","did":"Compared SHIFT to a concept bottleneck baseline, the only reasonable baseline they could think of under the task's data assumptions.","alternatives_named":["standard unlearning","spurious correlation removal techniques"],"stated_reason":"Standard unlearning and spurious correlation removal assume access to data isolating the spurious cue, which the task does not provide.","quote":"We compared this to a concept bottleneck baseline, which was the only reasonable baseline we could think of that could function under the task assumptions."},{"point":"D6","problem":"How strong a baseline standard to demand when claiming an interpretability method beats alternatives.","did":"Stated that one must beat the best baseline that exists, not merely the best known to the authors.","alternatives_named":["Beating only the best baseline you know of"],"stated_reason":"A later-discovered simple baseline was competitive with SHIFT, showing that known baselines can understate the true bar.","quote":"And I think that it's important that you beat the best baseline that exists, not just the best one that you know of."},{"point":"D1","problem":"Which tier of downstream demonstration (fair fight, no holds barred, in the wild) to recommend interpretability researchers aim for.","did":"Recommended fair-fight demos, even toy ones, rather than no-holds-barred or in-the-wild demos.","alternatives_named":["No holds barred demos","In the wild demos"],"stated_reason":"Fair fight demos capture most of the validation benefit, while harder tiers raise questions about whether the problems occur naturally, which can partly be handled by conceptual forecasting arguments.","quote":"My view is that \"fair fight\" demos capture most of the \"validating insights\" benefits."},{"point":"D5","problem":"How to interpret SHIFT's result given that it was a fair-fight demo.","did":"Acknowledged SHIFT would not beat a no-holds-barred baseline such as collecting synthetic data isolating gender, and so classified it only as a fair fight.","alternatives_named":["Claiming SHIFT as a no holds barred win"],"stated_reason":"Baselines like collecting auxiliary data isolating the gender concept would most certainly beat SHIFT.","quote":"The SHIFT demo I discussed above is a fair fight, but *not* no holds barred."}]}
